planting.note: Divide established mats in spring into lean, sharply drained sandy or sandhill soil in full sun; never amend with fertility, since garden loam will kill it faster than drought.

directions: A true xeric-sand specialist that fills the opposite niche from the garden's existing shade spikemosses, this fine-textured, drought-proof evergreen mat suits infertile, sun-baked sandy soil where almost nothing else groundcovers. Once established it needs no supplemental irrigation and resents wet feet, so it's best used in restoration plantings, sand gardens, or as a living mulch between cacti and yuccas. It is ranked vulnerable in parts of its range, so source nursery-propagated material only.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Divide into consistently wet to mesic, calcareous soil at a pond edge, bog-garden margin, or rain-garden toe-slope.

directions: The most cold-hardy spikemoss candidate in this collection, with a boreal range reaching into Quebec and Ontario, this species fills a gap for a zone-3-hardy spikemoss suited to bog gardens, fen restorations, and rain-garden margins in calcareous soil. It is a fen and swamp-margin species that struggles in acidic or dry conditions, so keep soil moisture constant through the growing season. It tolerates light shade from adjacent sedges and shrubs.

planting.note: Divide into crevices, scree, or unimproved native soil; explicitly intolerant of amended garden soil, so avoid prepared beds.

directions: Unusual among spikemosses for its erect, clump-forming habit rather than mat-forming, this species also stands out for genuinely wide light tolerance, rated from full coastal sun through deep oak-canopy shade. That flexibility makes it a good texture filler for rock gardens and naturalistic dry-shade plantings under oaks across its California and Baja range. Avoid overwatering, since it is adapted to summer drought.

planting.note: Divide nursery-propagated mats into clay or loam soil under the dappled shade of chaparral or coastal-sage shrubs.

directions: A shade-tolerant, resurrection-type mat species that grays and curls when dry, then greens when moist, distinct from the resurrection types already in the collection, this spikemoss serves as a drought-adapted groundcover under larger shrubs in coastal sage scrub gardens. It will bleach gray-brown and appear dormant during dry spells, then green back up within a day or two of rain or irrigation, a useful weather-indicator groundcover for xeriscape designs. Because of its limited range and watch-list status, use only nursery-propagated stock.

subcategory: alpine and prairie rock garden spikemoss

planting.note: Divide into rocky, gravelly, or sandy well-drained soil in full sun; plant generously spaced divisions, since this species is notably slow to spread, roughly 0.4 inches per year.

directions: The hardiest and most cold-tough spikemoss available for Great Plains and Rocky Mountain rock and alpine-trough gardens, this species is a natural dominant of shortgrass prairie and exposed alpine rock, proven in harsh, windy, snow-scoured sites. It is exceptionally drought and cold tolerant but very slow to spread, so expect a multi-year establishment period rather than a single-season fill-in. Best suited to alpine troughs, scree gardens, and xeric rock gardens in cold-winter climates where few other evergreen groundcovers survive.
sources: US Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

subcategory: Gulf Coast calcareous seep shade spikemoss

planting.note: Divide nursery-propagated mats into consistently moist, alkaline to neutral soil in open shade; do not let the soil dry out, which it does not tolerate.

directions: A genuine true-shade spikemoss for the humid Southeast, growing in open shade over moist, calcareous seeps and hammocks, this species carries a juniper-like ferny mat habit resembling a miniature blue rug juniper. Its long, sparsely branched creeping stems form a flat, fine-textured mat well suited as foreground groundcover under shade shrubs or along shaded limestone rock gardens in warm, humid climates. It is ranked vulnerable through most of its range, so source only nursery-propagated material.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
